sections.title: The man who drowned a typeface
sections.intro_md:
On a night in late August 1916, a 76-year-old bookbinder named Thomas Cobden-Sanderson walked onto Hammersmith Bridge in west London carrying a heavy bundle, and dropped it into the Thames. Inside were pieces of metal type. He came back again and again over the following months until every letter of the Doves Type, the typeface of his private press, lay in the river mud. His business partner had a claim on the type. Cobden-Sanderson preferred that nobody should have it.

Nobody throws Arial off a bridge. So why did a typeface matter that much to one man? And why, a century later, does the font on a memo still make headlines in Washington? That is today's question: what typography is actually for. The short answer is that it makes language visible and easy to take in. The long answer runs from Roman chisels to your phone, through road signs, courtrooms, ballots, and a cartoon dog.

spotlights.name: The Doves Type
spotlights.spot_it: A calm, slightly heavy roman type, modelled on Nicolas Jenson's 1470s letters, used for the Doves Bible.
spotlights.story_md: The Doves Press printed some of the most admired books of the Arts and Crafts movement, including a five-volume English Bible set only in this one size of type. When the partners Cobden-Sanderson and Emery Walker fell out, a legal agreement said the type would pass to Walker when Cobden-Sanderson died. Cobden-Sanderson made sure there was nothing to pass. He recorded the drops in his journal and called it a bequest to the river. In 2014 the designer Robert Green, who had spent years redrawing the face digitally, searched the riverbed below the bridge with Port of London Authority divers and brought up about 150 pieces. Most of the rest is thought to lie under later concrete repairs.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a typeface is something people own, fight over, and love, not just a setting in a menu.
spotlights.memory_hook: A typeface so precious its maker gave it to the river rather than to his partner.

spotlights.name: The Crystal Goblet
spotlights.spot_it: The metaphor every type student meets: wine in a clear glass versus wine in a golden cup.
spotlights.story_md: Beatrice Warde, an American who ran publicity for the Monotype Corporation in London, gave a talk to the British Typographers' Guild at the St Bride Institute. She asked listeners to imagine two goblets: one of solid gold, beautifully worked, and one of thin, clear crystal. A true wine lover, she said, picks the crystal, because everything about it reveals the wine instead of hiding it. Printing, she argued, should be like that glass: a window between the reader and the author's words, not a decoration that makes you look at the window. The talk was printed days later and has been reprinted ever since. Warde also wrote under a man's name, Paul Beaujon, so that her scholarship on type history would be taken seriously.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest single answer to what typography is for, and the one everyone else argues with.
spotlights.memory_hook: Good type is a clean wine glass: you notice the wine, not the glass.

sections.title: What typography is, in a few numbers
sections.intro_md:
Typography is the craft of arranging type so written language is legible, readable and fitting. Those three words do different jobs. Legibility is whether you can tell one letter from another: is that an l, an I or a 1? Readability is whether a page of text can be read for an hour without strain, which depends on line length, spacing and size more than on the letters themselves. Fitness is whether the type feels right for the message: a funeral notice and a birthday flyer should not look alike.

A typographer makes dozens of small choices: which typeface, what size, how long the lines are, how much space between lines, how headings stand apart, where the eye goes first. Most readers never notice any of it. They notice only when it goes wrong, which is why Warde called good typography invisible. The numbers below are the ones that frame the whole field today.

spotlights.name: Typeface versus font
spotlights.spot_it: Typeface is the design (Garamond). Font is one specific set of it (Garamond Italic, 12 point).
spotlights.story_md: In a print shop, a font was a physical thing: a case of metal letters of one style and one size, with more e's than z's, ready to be set by hand. The typeface was the design that all those fonts shared. The words blurred when computers arrived, because one digital file could print at any size. Designers still use the old distinction: a typeface is like a song, a font is like a particular recording of it. A family groups the variants of one typeface, such as light, regular, bold and italic. Today a single variable font file can hold an entire family, sliding smoothly from thin to black.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Knowing the difference lets you talk precisely about what you are choosing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Typeface is the song, font is the recording.

spotlights.name: Measure and leading
spotlights.when: Rules settled in book printing, restated by Robert Bringhurst in 1992
spotlights.spot_it: Line length (the measure) and the gap between lines (leading) decide whether a page feels easy or exhausting.
spotlights.story_md: Lines that are too long make the eye lose its place on the return trip to the next line. Lines that are too short break up phrases and force constant jumps. Robert Bringhurst's handbook The Elements of Typographic Style puts a comfortable single column at 45 to 75 characters, with 66 as the classic ideal. Leading, pronounced like the metal, comes from the thin strips of lead that hand compositors slipped between lines of type to open them up. Longer lines need more leading, so the eye can find its way back. Many websites still break these rules with lines of 120 characters or more across a wide screen.
spotlights.why_it_matters: These two settings change reading comfort more than the choice of typeface does.
spotlights.memory_hook: Leading is literally lead: strips of metal between the lines.

sections.title: How to look at a letter
sections.intro_md:
Typographers name the parts of letters the way doctors name bones, because you cannot compare designs without words for what differs. The baseline is the invisible line letters sit on. The x-height is the height of a lowercase x, and it decides how big a typeface looks at a given size. Ascenders rise above it (b, d, h), descenders drop below it (g, p, y). The enclosed space inside an o or a is the counter. A serif is the small stroke at the end of a main stroke. Stroke contrast is the difference between thick and thin parts.

These details are not decoration. A large x-height and open counters help a face survive small sizes and poor screens. Strong contrast looks elegant in a magazine headline and falls apart in tiny captions. Once you can see these parts, you start noticing why one menu, sign or app feels easy and another feels cramped.

spotlights.name: The serif
spotlights.when: Visible on Roman inscriptions by the 1st and 2nd centuries
spotlights.spot_it: Tiny cross-strokes at the ends of letters, like the feet on the T in Times New Roman.
spotlights.story_md: Where serifs come from is still argued. The best known theory, from the priest and calligrapher Edward Catich in 1968, says Roman sign writers painted letters onto stone with a flat brush before carving, and the brush naturally left flared ends that the carvers then cut. Older theories said the chisel itself needed clean stopping points. Either way, the serif stayed for two thousand years. Faces without serifs, called sans serif, appeared in British printing around 1816 and were long called grotesques because they looked so bare. The common rule that serifs guide the eye along the line has never been shown reliably in experiments.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the first thing anyone uses to sort typefaces, and its origin is a real historical puzzle.
spotlights.memory_hook: Serifs may be brush marks frozen in stone.

spotlights.name: The x-height
spotlights.when: Term in use since the metal-type era
spotlights.spot_it: Compare the height of a lowercase x with a capital: the taller the x, the bigger the face looks.
spotlights.story_md: Two typefaces set at the same point size can look very different in size, because point size measures the whole metal body, not the visible letter. Times New Roman has a modest x-height. Verdana and Georgia, designed for early screens, have very large ones, so they read clearly at small sizes on coarse pixels. That is also why swapping one font for another at the same size can make a document run a page longer or shorter. Designers of signs, medicine labels and phone interfaces pay close attention to x-height for this reason.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It explains why 11 point in one font is not the same as 11 point in another.
spotlights.memory_hook: Point size measures the box, x-height measures the letter.

spotlights.name: Kerning and ligatures
spotlights.when: Kerned metal sorts by the 1600s; ligatures from medieval scribes
spotlights.spot_it: Kerning tucks letters like A and V closer; a ligature fuses letters like f and i into one shape.
spotlights.story_md: Every letter has default space on each side, but some pairs look wrong at those defaults. AV, To and LT leave visible holes, so typefaces carry thousands of kerning pairs that adjust specific combinations. In metal type, a kern was literally a piece of the letter that hung over the edge of its block. Ligatures solve a different problem: in many serif faces the hook of an f collides with the dot of an i, so printers cast fi and fl as single pieces. The ampersand, &, began as a ligature of the Latin word et. Bad kerning has its own internet name, keming, because the r and n in kerning can run together into an m.
spotlights.why_it_matters: These invisible fixes are a large part of why professional type looks smooth.
spotlights.memory_hook: Kerning badly turns kerning into keming.

sections.title: From chisels to movable type
sections.intro_md:
Typography begins before type. Roman stone carvers worked out the proportions of capital letters that designers still copy. Scribes in monasteries, mosques and scriptoria developed page layouts, margins and columns long before printing. Then came the big idea: make each letter a separate, reusable piece, arrange the pieces into a page, print, and rearrange.

That idea was invented more than once. In China, Bi Sheng made movable type from baked clay around the 1040s. In Korea, metal type printed a Buddhist text in 1377, about 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible. What Johannes Gutenberg added in Mainz in the 1450s was a whole system: a hand mould that cast thousands of identical metal letters quickly, an oil-based ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press adapted from wine and paper making. That system, not a single invention, let printing spread across Europe within fifty years.

spotlights.name: The Trajan inscription
spotlights.spot_it: Square-cut Roman capitals on the base of a 30-metre column in Rome, with crisp serifs and graceful proportions.
spotlights.story_md: The panel at the base of Trajan's Column is probably the most studied piece of lettering in the world. Its capitals are carved in V-shaped cuts that catch light and shadow. Type designers from the Renaissance to today have measured it, and in 1989 Carol Twombly drew the typeface Trajan for Adobe directly from it. Trajan has capitals only, like the original, because Romans did not use lowercase. It became so common on film posters, for dramas and thrillers alike, that it is now a cliche of Hollywood marketing. The column itself was finished in 113 CE to celebrate the emperor Trajan's wars in Dacia.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Our capital letters are still, more or less, the ones on this stone.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's most copied font has been standing in Rome for 1,900 years.

spotlights.name: Bi Sheng and clay type
spotlights.spot_it: Small baked clay blocks, one character each, set into an iron frame held by wax and resin.
spotlights.story_md: Almost everything we know about Bi Sheng comes from one paragraph in the Dream Pool Essays by the scholar Shen Kuo, written around 1088. Bi Sheng, described as a commoner, carved characters into soft clay, baked them hard, and set them in an iron frame coated with a mix of pine resin, wax and paper ash. Heating the frame softened the wax so the type could be pressed flat; cooling it locked everything in place. Two frames let one be printed while the other was set. For a script with thousands of characters, movable type gave less advantage than in alphabets, so carved woodblocks remained common in China for centuries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Movable type was a Chinese invention, four centuries before Mainz.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first movable type was baked like pottery.

spotlights.name: Jikji
spotlights.spot_it: A thin Korean Buddhist book in Chinese characters, with the colophon noting it was printed with cast metal type.
spotlights.story_md: Jikji, a selection of teachings of Buddhist masters, was printed at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju in 1377. It is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, about 78 years before the Gutenberg Bible. Only the second volume survives, and it is not in Korea: it was bought in Seoul by a French diplomat in the 1880s and is now held by the Bibliothèque nationale de France in Paris, which Korea has long asked to return. UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World register in 2001. The Korean scholar Park Byeong-seon identified its significance while working at the French library in 1972.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proves that metal movable type existed in Asia before Europe.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's oldest metal-type book lives in Paris, not Korea.

spotlights.name: The Gutenberg Bible
spotlights.spot_it: Two dense columns of black Gothic letters, 42 lines per column, with red and blue initials added by hand.
spotlights.story_md: Gutenberg's workshop printed about 180 copies, about 145 on paper and 35 on vellum, which needed the skins of roughly 170 calves per copy by common estimates. Gutenberg wanted the book to look like the finest handwritten manuscripts, so his type imitated a scribe's textura, including about 290 different pieces for letters, ligatures and abbreviations, far more than the alphabet needs. Lines are justified to an even right edge, partly thanks to those alternative shorter forms. Forty-nine copies survived into the 20th century, 21 of them complete. The Library of Congress holds one of three perfect vellum copies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the standard that printed books matched the beauty of manuscripts, not just their content.
spotlights.memory_hook: The first great printed book worked hard to look handwritten.

spotlights.name: Nicolas Jenson's roman
spotlights.spot_it: Open, even lowercase letters with modest serifs, the ancestor of almost every book type you read.
spotlights.story_md: Jenson was a Frenchman, possibly trained at the royal mint, who set up as a printer in Venice. His 1470 edition of Eusebius used a roman type based on the handwriting of Italian humanist scholars, who had revived an older, clearer script and paired it with Roman capitals. Jenson's version was so balanced that William Morris copied it in the 1890s, the Doves Press built its type on it, and digital revivals such as Adobe Jenson exist today. When people say a type looks classical, they usually mean it descends from these Venetian pages.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The everyday lowercase roman of books was fixed here.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your paperback's letters were born in Venice in 1470.

sections.title: Four faces that shaped the book
sections.intro_md:
After Jenson, type design moved in recognisable steps, and you can learn to see them. Old-style faces, from Venice and later Paris, have a slanted axis, as if drawn with a broad pen held at an angle, and gentle contrast. Transitional faces of the 1700s, led by John Baskerville in Birmingham, stood the axis upright and sharpened the contrast. Modern faces, perfected by Bodoni in Parma and the Didot family in Paris around 1800, pushed contrast to hairline thin strokes against heavy verticals.

Each step tracked new technology: smoother paper, better ink, sharper presses. Each also carried a mood. Old-style feels warm and literary. Transitional feels crisp and rational, the Enlightenment in letters. Modern feels glamorous and cold, which is why fashion magazines still love it. The italic, meanwhile, began as a separate type for small portable books, and only later became the partner of the roman.

spotlights.name: Aldus and the first italic
spotlights.spot_it: Slanted, narrow, flowing letters across the page of a small book, with roman capitals.
spotlights.story_md: Aldus Manutius ran the most ambitious press in Renaissance Venice. In 1501 he printed an edition of Virgil in a small format, roughly the size of a modern paperback, set in a new slanted type cut by Francesco Griffo and based on fast humanist handwriting. The narrow letters fitted more words on a page, which kept the books cheap and portable. Aldus also printed the Hypnerotomachia Poliphili in 1499, often called the most beautiful book of the Renaissance, and popularised the semicolon. His anchor and dolphin mark is still used by publishers today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The pocket book and the italic arrived together.
spotlights.memory_hook: Italic was invented to squeeze Virgil into your pocket.

spotlights.name: Garamond
spotlights.spot_it: Graceful old-style roman with a small x-height and long ascenders; the default face of countless novels.
spotlights.story_md: Claude Garamond was one of the first people to make a living mainly by cutting punches for type rather than printing. His romans became the standard of European printing for two centuries. Many fonts called Garamond today are not based on his work at all: in the 1920s it emerged that several revivals were actually copied from types made about 80 years later by Jean Jannon, which the French national printing office had mislabelled. Beatrice Warde, writing as Paul Beaujon, published that discovery in 1926. A popular 2014 claim that the US government could save millions by switching to Garamond was later questioned, because Garamond looks smaller at the same point size.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the model of the quiet, readable book face.
spotlights.memory_hook: Half the Garamonds are not Garamond, and Warde caught it.

spotlights.name: John Baskerville
spotlights.spot_it: Upright, crisp letters with sharp contrast and a famous curly lowercase g with an open lower loop.
spotlights.story_md: Baskerville made his fortune in japanned lacquer goods before turning to printing in his forties. Obsessed with perfection, he improved the press, developed blacker ink and had smoother paper made, which allowed finer strokes. His 1757 Virgil impressed collectors abroad more than in Britain, where rivals claimed his sharp type would hurt readers' eyes. Benjamin Franklin, a fan, played a joke on one critic: he tore the heading off a specimen by another founder, said it was Baskerville, and the critic dutifully found it painful to read. The story reached us through Franklin's own letter to Baskerville in 1760.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He bridged the old-style and the modern face, and showed that paper and ink are part of typography.
spotlights.memory_hook: Franklin proved Baskerville's critics were reading the label, not the letters.

spotlights.name: Giambattista Bodoni
spotlights.spot_it: Extreme contrast: hairline serifs and thin strokes against bold verticals; looks like a fashion masthead.
spotlights.story_md: Bodoni ran the ducal press in Parma and cut tens of thousands of punches in his career. His aim was sharp, dramatic pages with a lot of white space, more for display than for long reading. His widow, Margherita Dall'Aglio, published his Manuale Tipografico in 1818, showing well over a hundred roman alphabets plus italics, Greek, Hebrew and more. The same style, developed in parallel by the Didot family in Paris, is the ancestor of the logos of Vogue and Harper's Bazaar. The thin hairlines need good paper and careful printing, which is why Bodoni looks stunning large and weak at small sizes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Contrast became a mood: high contrast now signals luxury.
spotlights.memory_hook: When you see a fashion logo, you see Bodoni's ghost.

sections.title: Machines that changed how words look
sections.intro_md:
For four hundred years, every line of print was assembled by hand, one letter at a time, from wooden cases: capitals in the upper case and small letters in the lower case, which is where those words come from. Even a fast compositor could set only a few columns a day, and a daily newspaper needed dozens of columns by midnight.

The machines that followed changed not only speed but the look of words. Hot-metal line-casting made daily papers and cheap books possible. The typewriter put a printing press on every office desk, but its fixed letter widths forced ugly compromises and created habits we still argue about. Then the personal computer handed typography to everyone, along with menus full of fonts and no training in using them. Each jump made type cheaper, faster and more personal, and each one produced a backlash from people who missed the craft.

spotlights.name: The Linotype machine
spotlights.spot_it: A tall, clanking machine with a 90-key keyboard that casts a whole line of type as one metal slug.
spotlights.story_md: Ottmar Mergenthaler, a German immigrant in Baltimore, built a machine that let an operator type a line, assemble brass letter moulds called matrices, and cast the line in molten lead as a single bar. It was first used at the New-York Tribune in 1886. One operator could do the work of several hand compositors, and after use the lead was melted down and reused. Linotype ran most of the world's newspapers until the 1970s. The keyboard was arranged by letter frequency, and operators fixing a mistake would run a finger down the first two columns, producing etaoin shrdlu, a nonsense phrase that sometimes slipped into print.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made the cheap daily newspaper possible and shaped a century of news type.
spotlights.memory_hook: etaoin shrdlu: the scar of a typo in hot lead.

spotlights.name: The typewriter
spotlights.spot_it: Monospaced letters: every character, from i to m, gets the same width, and underlining stands in for italics.
spotlights.story_md: The typewriter made every office a small printing shop, but with crude tools. Because each letter took the same width, an i looked lonely and an m looked squeezed. There was no italic, so people underlined; no bold, so they typed in capitals; no real quotation marks. Many typists were taught to put two spaces after a full stop. Typewriters also brought the QWERTY keyboard, which outlived them. When word processors arrived, they inherited typewriter habits, and the argument over one space or two after a full stop is still running in offices and style guides.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Many bad typographic habits are typewriter workarounds that outlived the machine.
spotlights.memory_hook: Underlining is italics for people who had no italics.

spotlights.name: The Macintosh and Steve Jobs' calligraphy class
spotlights.spot_it: A small beige computer whose screen showed menus in Chicago, a bold bitmap font, and could switch between named fonts.
spotlights.story_md: In his 2005 Stanford commencement speech, Steve Jobs said that after dropping out of Reed College he sat in on a calligraphy class, learning about serif and sans serif type and varying the space between letter combinations. Ten years later, he said, it all came back to him when designing the first Macintosh. The 1984 Mac offered proportional fonts on screen, named after cities: Chicago, Geneva, New York, Monaco. Most were drawn pixel by pixel by the designer Susan Kare, who also made the Mac's icons. Within two years, the Mac, laser printers and page layout software had launched desktop publishing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It put typeface choice in the hands of ordinary people for the first time.
spotlights.memory_hook: A dropout's calligraphy class ended up on every computer.

sections.title: The modernists and the faces that went everywhere
sections.intro_md:
In the 1920s a group of young designers in Germany, Switzerland and the Soviet Union declared that the old ornamented page was dead. Type should be as functional as a machine: sans serif, asymmetric, set on clear grids, with nothing that did not do a job. Their manifestos produced Futura, the Bauhaus look and, after the Second World War, the Swiss style of Helvetica and strict grids that corporate design adopted worldwide.

At the same time, a newspaper in London commissioned a serif that would become the most used typeface of the 20th century. These two strands, the clean sans and the efficient serif, still dominate what you read. Their stories show something important about what typography is for: the same face can feel neutral to one generation and loaded with meaning to the next.

spotlights.name: Jan Tschichold
spotlights.spot_it: Asymmetric pages, sans serif type, bold rules; later, the calm, centred covers of Penguin paperbacks.
spotlights.story_md: Tschichold was a sign painter's son from Leipzig who became the loudest voice of the new typography. His 1928 book Die neue Typographie demanded sans serif type and asymmetric layouts. In 1933 the Nazis arrested him as a cultural Bolshevik, and he fled to Switzerland. There he changed his mind: he came to see his old dogmatism as uncomfortably close to the authoritarian thinking he had escaped, and returned to classical, centred layouts. From 1947 to 1949 he redesigned Penguin Books, writing the Penguin Composition Rules that standardised hundreds of titles. His career shows a designer arguing with himself about what type is for.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He wrote the modernist rulebook and then its sharpest critique.
spotlights.memory_hook: The prophet of new typography became the reformer of old-fashioned paperbacks.

spotlights.name: Futura
spotlights.spot_it: Geometric sans: a perfectly round o, pointed A, M and N, and a tiny lowercase x-height.
spotlights.story_md: Paul Renner built Futura from circles, triangles and squares, in tune with the Bauhaus, though he was never part of the school. It became one of the most used faces of the century, for Volkswagen, IKEA's old catalogues and countless posters. In July 1969 Futura went to the Moon: the plaque left by Apollo 11, reading Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, is set in it. NASA used Futura widely in the 1960s. Stanley Kubrick used it for the titles of 2001: A Space Odyssey, and Wes Anderson uses it so often it has become his signature.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the face that made geometric modernism feel like the future.
spotlights.memory_hook: The only typeface on the Moon is Futura.

spotlights.name: Helvetica
spotlights.spot_it: Tight, horizontal stroke endings, a square-ish R with a vertical leg, a t with a flat top.
spotlights.story_md: Max Miedinger and Eduard Hoffmann of the Haas foundry near Basel released it as Neue Haas Grotesk in 1957. The German owner Stempel renamed it Helvetica, from the Latin name of Switzerland, so it would sell abroad. It became the face of corporate modernism: American Airlines, Lufthansa, Jeep, the New York subway signs from 1989 standards onward, and Apple's interfaces for years. Gary Hustwit's 2007 documentary Helvetica turned it into a pop subject. Its fans call it neutral; its critics, like the designer Erik Spiekermann, call it boring, and some call it the face of power. Both sides agree you cannot avoid it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a face can come to stand for an entire attitude.
spotlights.memory_hook: Helvetica means Swiss, and it is everywhere you look.

spotlights.name: Times New Roman
spotlights.spot_it: A compact, sharp serif with short ascenders, designed to fit more words in narrow newspaper columns.
spotlights.story_md: In 1929 Stanley Morison, adviser to the Monotype Corporation, wrote a critique of The Times's printing, and the paper asked him to fix it. He supervised the draughtsman Victor Lardent, who drew the face based on an older Plantin type. Times New Roman debuted on 3 October 1932. The Times itself dropped it in 1972, but by then it was everywhere in books and magazines. Microsoft made it the default in Word and Windows for years, which turned it into the face of school essays and legal filings. Many courts and governments still require it, and it went back into the US State Department in December 2025.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It became the global default for formal documents.
spotlights.memory_hook: A newspaper face designed to save space became the font of homework.

sections.title: Type at 100 kilometres an hour
sections.intro_md:
On a road sign, typography is a safety device. A driver at motorway speed has a second or two to read a place name, and a misread exit can kill. Sign typefaces are therefore some of the most tested in the world, and their designers think hard about letter shapes that stay distinct when seen at a distance, at night, in rain or by older eyes.

The British system designed by Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert in the late 1950s and early 1960s is the classic case: mixed upper and lowercase letters, which form more recognisable word shapes at a distance than all capitals, on colour-coded panels. Its approach spread across the former British Empire and beyond, including to signs in parts of India and the Gulf. The American story is messier, with a decade-long fight over whether a new highway font was any better than the old one.

spotlights.name: Johnston's Underground alphabet
spotlights.spot_it: Clean sans serif capitals on the red, white and blue London Underground roundel; a diamond-shaped dot on the i.
spotlights.story_md: Frank Pick, the Underground's publicity manager, wanted lettering that looked plainly modern and could not be mistaken for advertising on crowded platforms. He commissioned the calligrapher Edward Johnston, who based the proportions of his sans serif on classical Roman capitals. It was first used in 1916, making it one of the oldest corporate typefaces still in use. Johnston's pupil Eric Gill later developed Gill Sans from it. Transport for London still uses a digital descendant, Johnston100, redrawn in 2016 for the face's centenary.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved that a typeface can be a city's identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: London's tube has been speaking the same typeface for over a century.

spotlights.name: Transport and the British road sign
spotlights.spot_it: White mixed-case sans serif on blue motorway signs and green primary route signs, with a curled tail on the l.
spotlights.story_md: Jock Kinneir and his former student Margaret Calvert were hired to design signs for Britain's first motorway, the Preston Bypass, opened in 1958. They chose lowercase with capitals, rather than all capitals, and tested letters on signs propped against trees in Hyde Park and on boards driven past volunteers on an airfield. Their typeface, Transport, became the national standard on 1 January 1965. Calvert also drew many of the pictograms, including the schoolchildren crossing sign, in which the girl is based on a photograph of herself as a child. She kept designing type well into her eighties.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It turned road signs into a calm, readable national system.
spotlights.memory_hook: The girl on the British school crossing sign is Margaret Calvert herself.

spotlights.name: Highway Gothic versus Clearview
spotlights.spot_it: Highway Gothic is the narrow, blocky American sign face; Clearview has larger, more open lowercase letters.
spotlights.story_md: American highways have used the FHWA alphabets, nicknamed Highway Gothic, since the 1940s. In the 1990s the designers Donald Meeker and James Montalbano developed Clearview, partly because older drivers struggled with glowing letters at night, where bright strokes bleed into the counters. Early tests suggested better reading distances, and the FHWA gave it interim approval in 2004. In January 2016 the agency withdrew it, citing research that it read worse on dark-background signs. Congress then ordered the approval restored in the 2018 spending law, and an FHWA memo did so in March 2018. The fight shows how hard it is to prove a typeface is better.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Legibility claims need careful testing, and results depend on conditions.
spotlights.memory_hook: America changed its highway font twice in fourteen years.

spotlights.name: Frutiger at Charles de Gaulle Airport
spotlights.spot_it: A humanist sans: open shapes, slight stroke contrast, letters that stay readable from an angle and a distance.
spotlights.story_md: The Swiss designer Adrian Frutiger, already famous for Univers, was asked to design signs for the new Paris airport, which opened in 1974. He found Univers looked too static and tight at a distance, so he drew a new alphabet with more open letters and clearer shapes. Released commercially in 1976 as Frutiger, it became one of the most used sign faces in the world, in hospitals, transport systems and the Swiss road network for a time. Airports remain a key test of typography, because tired, stressed travellers reading a foreign language need to find a gate fast.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows wayfinding type being designed from the reader's situation outward.
spotlights.memory_hook: Frutiger designed for people running late for a plane.

sections.title: What the reading research actually says
sections.intro_md:
Typography is full of confident rules: serifs are easier to read on paper, sans serif on screens, we read words by their outline shape, special fonts help people with dyslexia, harder fonts help you remember. When researchers test these rules properly, most of them shrink or vanish.

What holds up is less glamorous. Size, contrast, spacing, line length and familiarity matter more than the style of a typeface. People read fastest in what they are used to. Very unusual letters slow everyone down at first. And the mood of a face does seem to change how people judge what it says, even when they do not notice the face at all. This section is about separating the craft wisdom that survives testing from the parts that are folklore.

data.claim: We read words by their outline shape
data.evidence: Recognition runs on letters in parallel (Larson, 2004)
No benefit from letterforms; spacing effects mixed (Kuster 2017; Galliussi 2020)
Sans Forgetica: no benefit in 3 preregistered studies (2020)
No consistent difference at normal sizes
Baskerville nudged agreement in a 45,000 reader online test (2012)

spotlights.name: The word shape myth
spotlights.spot_it: The claim that we recognise whole words by their outline, like a skyline of tall and short letters.
spotlights.story_md: For decades, designers argued that all-capital text was hard to read because it destroys word shapes, the bumpy outlines known as Bouma shapes. In 2004 Kevin Larson, a psychologist on Microsoft's typography team, reviewed the research and argued that the evidence pointed elsewhere. Readers recognise the letters within a word in parallel, very fast, and use that to identify the word. Lowercase still reads a little faster than capitals, but mostly because we practise it far more. Larson pointed to experiments in which changing letters mattered far more than changing outline shape, and to eye-tracking work showing readers pick up letter information from the next word before their eyes land on it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It corrects one of the most repeated explanations in design teaching.
spotlights.memory_hook: You read letters very fast, not outlines.

spotlights.name: Fonts for dyslexia
spotlights.spot_it: Letters with heavy bottoms and exaggerated differences between b, d, p and q, plus wide spacing.
spotlights.story_md: Several fonts claim to help readers with dyslexia by making letters harder to flip or confuse. The research is unkind to the claim. In 2017 a Dutch study of 170 children found that Dyslexie did not improve reading for children with or without dyslexia. A small 2017 American study found OpenDyslexic did not improve speed or accuracy either. Later work suggests that any small gains come from wider spacing, which can be applied to ordinary fonts, and even spacing effects are mixed. Researchers do not say the fonts are harmful: if a child likes one, fine. They warn against spending money or hope that should go to proven reading instruction.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Good intentions do not replace testing, even in typography.
spotlights.memory_hook: The magic is in the spacing, if anywhere, not the letters.

spotlights.name: Sans Forgetica
spotlights.spot_it: A back-slanting font with gaps cut out of every letter, so the reader must fill them in.
spotlights.story_md: In 2018 researchers and designers at RMIT University in Melbourne released a font designed to be just hard enough to read that it would make information stick. The idea came from a respected theory of desirable difficulty: effort during learning can improve memory. The launch got worldwide press. Then independent researchers tested it. In 2020 three preregistered experiments by Jonathan Geller and colleagues found no memory benefit at all. A later study found a small effect only when students did not expect a test, which is rarely how real studying works. The episode is a neat example of a plausible story outrunning the evidence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows why typography claims need replication, not press releases.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sans Forgetica was forgettable as a memory aid.

spotlights.name: Errol Morris's Baskerville test
spotlights.spot_it: An online quiz where the same passage appeared, at random, in one of six typefaces.
spotlights.story_md: The filmmaker Errol Morris ran a disguised experiment on the New York Times website. About 45,000 readers read a passage arguing that we live in an unusually safe era, then said whether they agreed. Unknown to them, the text appeared in Baskerville, Computer Modern, Georgia, Helvetica, Comic Sans or Trebuchet. Baskerville drew the highest agreement and the lowest disagreement; Comic Sans did worst. The effect was small, a few percentage points, and Morris admitted it was not a formal study. Still, it hints at something designers have long believed: readers judge credibility partly by the clothes the words wear.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It gives rare numbers to the idea that type carries tone.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same words, different font, different belief.

sections.title: Type has a tone of voice
sections.intro_md:
If typography were only about legibility, any clear face would do for any message. In practice, people react to typefaces the way they react to voices. A wedding invitation in a stencil army font, or a cancer charity leaflet in a cartoon face, feels wrong even to someone who could not name either font.

This is the second job of typography, after making text readable: matching the words to the moment. Designers talk about connotation, the associations a face has picked up from where it has been used. Those associations are learned, not built in, and they shift. Here are three cases where the tone of a typeface became the story.

spotlights.name: Comic Sans
spotlights.spot_it: Rounded, wobbly, hand-lettered capitals and lowercase, like a comic speech bubble.
spotlights.story_md: Vincent Connare, a typographic engineer at Microsoft, saw a test version of Microsoft Bob in October 1994. Its cartoon dog, Rover, spoke in speech bubbles set in Times New Roman, which Connare thought looked absurdly formal. He drew a casual face based on comic book lettering, including The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen, quickly. It was not finished in time for Bob, but it shipped in other Microsoft products and with Windows 95 add-ons, and so it landed on millions of computers. People used it for everything, including gravestones and legal notices, and a backlash campaign called Ban Comic Sans followed. Some teachers and readers with dyslexia like it, because its letters are distinct.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a good face for one job becomes a joke when used for every job.
spotlights.memory_hook: Comic Sans was born because a cartoon dog was talking in Times New Roman.

spotlights.name: The Higgs boson in Comic Sans
spotlights.spot_it: Physics slides announcing one of the century's biggest discoveries, in a cartoon font.
spotlights.story_md: When the physicist Fabiola Gianotti presented the ATLAS experiment's evidence for a new particle consistent with the Higgs boson, her slides were set in Comic Sans. For a few hours, the typeface competed with the discovery for attention online, and a joke petition asked Microsoft to rename it Comic CERNs. Two years later, CERN played along with an April Fools' announcement that it would switch all official communications to Comic Sans. Gianotti later became the first woman to lead CERN. The episode shows the gap between experts in one field and the norms of another: physicists cared about the data, designers about the font.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the best known case of a typeface clashing with the weight of a message.
spotlights.memory_hook: The God particle arrived dressed in Comic Sans.

spotlights.name: IKEA's switch to Verdana
spotlights.spot_it: IKEA signs and catalogues in a wide, plain screen font instead of the old Futura-based IKEA Sans.
spotlights.story_md: For decades IKEA used a custom version of Futura in its catalogues and stores. In 2009 it announced that its 2010 catalogue would switch to Verdana, Matthew Carter's screen font, so that the same face could be used in print, on its website and across many languages cheaply. Designers reacted with fury; Time magazine reported on the row, and online it was nicknamed Verdanagate. Critics said a font made for small text on screens looked clumsy at poster size. IKEA stuck with it for years before moving to a custom face, Noto IKEA, in 2019. The episode showed how much people feel brands are their letters.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Typeface changes can feel like a change of character to customers.
spotlights.memory_hook: Verdanagate: the day designers marched over a catalogue.

sections.title: Type for screens
sections.intro_md:
A screen is a hostile place for letters. Early displays had so few pixels that a lowercase e might be drawn with five dots across. Printed typefaces, designed for ink on paper, fell apart. The fix was a new kind of design: fonts built from the pixel grid upward, and hinting, the fiddly instructions that tell a font how to snap to pixels at each small size.

Then screens got sharper, and the web learned to download fonts instead of relying on the few installed on each computer. Today about 88% of websites load web fonts, and about a third use variable fonts that pack a whole family into one file. Typography became responsive: the same text reflows on a phone, a laptop and a watch, so designers now set rules rather than fixed pages. Each step changed what typography is for: from fixing words on paper to keeping them readable on any device.

visual.title: Variable fonts on the web (share of pages, approximate)

spotlights.name: Verdana and Georgia
spotlights.spot_it: Verdana: wide, open sans with roomy spacing. Georgia: a sturdy serif with old-style figures that dip below the line.
spotlights.story_md: Microsoft commissioned Matthew Carter to design two faces that would read well on the coarse screens of the mid-1990s. Unusually, Carter drew the pixel versions first and then the outlines, with Tom Rickner doing the painstaking hinting. Both have large x-heights and generous spacing so letters do not touch at small sizes. Microsoft gave them away free with its Core fonts for the Web project from 1996, which is why they appeared on so many early websites. Carter, born in 1937, also designed Bell Centennial for American phone books and started his career cutting metal punches by hand: few people have designed type across so many technologies.
spotlights.why_it_matters: They proved that screen type needed its own design, not adapted print faces.
spotlights.memory_hook: Carter drew the pixels before the curves.

spotlights.name: Emigre and the bitmap faces
spotlights.spot_it: Chunky, stair-stepped letters that embraced the pixel instead of hiding it.
spotlights.story_md: Zuzana Licko, a Czech-born designer, and her husband Rudy VanderLans started Emigre, a magazine and type foundry, the same year the Macintosh launched. Rather than imitate print faces on the low-resolution Mac, Licko designed fonts that celebrated pixels: Emperor, Oakland, Emigre. Later faces like Matrix and Mrs Eaves became widely used. Emigre's experimental layouts in the late 1980s and 1990s upset older designers, who called them illegible. Licko's reply became famous: we read best what we read most. Legibility, she argued, is partly habit, which matches what reading research later found.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It argued that readability is learned and can change.
spotlights.memory_hook: We read best what we read most.

spotlights.name: Variable fonts
spotlights.spot_it: Text that smoothly thickens, narrows or slants as you resize a window, from one font file.
spotlights.story_md: In 2016 Apple, Google, Microsoft and Adobe jointly announced OpenType variable fonts. Instead of separate files for light, regular, bold and so on, one file stores a design along axes such as weight, width and slant, and the computer can produce any point in between. That saves download size and lets text adapt to a screen: slightly heavier on a dim phone, narrower in a tight column. Google's Noto project, which aims to cover every script in Unicode so no text shows as empty boxes, uses the same technology. The empty boxes are nicknamed tofu, and Noto's name comes from no more tofu.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It makes type flexible enough for any screen and language.
spotlights.memory_hook: Noto means no more tofu.

sections.title: When type decided something big
sections.intro_md:
Most of the time, bad typography costs a little: a slower read, a confused customer, an ugly menu. Sometimes it decides outcomes. Ballots, legal documents and forensic evidence show typography at its most consequential, because layout and letterforms can change what people do and what courts believe.

These cases also show two odd uses of type. A badly laid out page can steer people into mistakes. And because every font has a release date, the font on a document can act like a timestamp, exposing a forgery the way carbon dating exposes a fake relic.

spotlights.name: The butterfly ballot
spotlights.spot_it: Candidate names on two facing pages with a single column of punch holes running down the middle.
spotlights.story_md: To use a larger print size for older voters, the county's election supervisor laid out the presidential ballot across two pages. Al Gore was the second name on the left, but his punch hole was the third in the centre column; the second hole belonged to Pat Buchanan, listed on the right. Buchanan received 3,407 votes in Palm Beach, an outlier compared with every other Florida county. A 2001 study in the American Political Science Review estimated that the design caused more than 2,000 Democratic voters to mark Buchanan by mistake, more than George W. Bush's statewide margin of 537. Buchanan himself said many of those votes were probably not meant for him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A layout decision may have changed a US presidential election.
spotlights.memory_hook: A design meant to help older eyes may have chosen a president.

spotlights.name: Fontgate: Calibri in the Panama Papers case
spotlights.spot_it: A trust deed dated 2006, typed in Calibri, the friendly rounded sans that became Microsoft Office's default in 2007.
spotlights.story_md: During Pakistan's investigation of Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's family after the Panama Papers leak, his daughter Maryam Nawaz submitted a trust deed dated February 2006. A London forensic document laboratory told the Joint Investigation Team the document was set in Calibri, which was not commercially available until January 2007. Supporters pointed out that test versions of Calibri had circulated earlier; the font's Wikipedia page was edited so often that it had to be locked. The Supreme Court disqualified Nawaz Sharif from office in July 2017 on other grounds, and the font question became a famous example of typographic forensics.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Every font has a birth date, which makes type a forensic clue.
spotlights.memory_hook: A font can be a timestamp that a forger forgets.

spotlights.name: The Killian documents
spotlights.spot_it: Memos supposedly typed in 1972-73, with a raised th and proportional spacing that matched modern Microsoft Word defaults.
spotlights.story_md: CBS's 60 Minutes Wednesday aired memos said to come from a commander of George W. Bush's National Guard unit in the early 1970s. Within hours, bloggers noticed that the memos looked like they were made in Word with default Times New Roman: proportional spacing, a curly apostrophe and a superscript th, features most 1970s office typewriters did not produce. Some typewriters could do some of these things, so the debate was not simple, but an independent panel later said CBS had failed to authenticate the memos. Producer Mary Mapes was fired and anchor Dan Rather left the evening news.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed how typographic detail can be read as evidence by anyone paying attention.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tiny raised th helped end a news anchor's run.

sections.title: Typography beyond the Latin alphabet
sections.intro_md:
Most typography history is told through Latin letters, but most of the world's readers use other scripts, and each poses different problems. Chinese needs thousands of characters, which made both movable type and the typewriter hard. Arabic letters join and change shape depending on their position, which metal type handled clumsily for centuries. Korean groups letters into syllable blocks. Devanagari hangs letters from a headline and stacks consonants into conjuncts.

These problems shaped history. Where type fitted a script badly, handwriting and woodblocks survived longer, and the arrival of computers was a bigger liberation. Today's technologies, Unicode for encoding and OpenType for shaping, finally let all scripts work on the same devices, though quality still varies widely between them.

data.solution: Large type cases; later, input by keys plus selection

data.challenge: Joined letters with up to four forms each
data.solution: Many sorts per letter; now OpenType shaping
Hundreds of sorts; now shaping engines

spotlights.name: Hangul, the designed alphabet
spotlights.spot_it: Simple strokes and circles grouped into square syllable blocks, such as 한글.
spotlights.story_md: King Sejong of Joseon and his scholars created Hangul so ordinary Koreans could read and write, instead of relying on Chinese characters that took years to learn. The book announcing it, Hunminjeongeum, explains that consonant shapes draw the position of the mouth and tongue when making the sound: the letter for k shows the tongue touching the back of the mouth. Its 1446 commentary, rediscovered in 1940, is on UNESCO's Memory of the World register. Korea celebrates Hangul Day each October. It is one of the very few scripts whose designers and design logic are documented.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a script designed for legibility and learning on purpose.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hangul's letters are diagrams of your mouth.

spotlights.name: The MingKwai typewriter
spotlights.spot_it: A compact typewriter with 72 keys for Chinese, where keys select character shapes and a small window shows the choices.
spotlights.story_md: Chinese typewriters before the 1940s were huge trays of thousands of metal characters picked one by one. The writer Lin Yutang spent much of his fortune on a different idea: keys for shapes of character parts, so that pressing a combination brought up a few candidate characters in a window, and the typist picked the right one. The machine, built with Mergenthaler Linotype in New York in 1947, failed to go into production. The only prototype vanished, until 2025, when a family clearing a basement in New York posted photos online. Historian Thomas Mullaney confirmed it, and it went to Stanford. Its select-from-candidates idea is how most people type Chinese on phones today.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It anticipated the input methods used by over a billion people.
spotlights.memory_hook: Your phone's Chinese keyboard was predicted by a lost typewriter found in a basement.

spotlights.name: İbrahim Müteferrika's press
spotlights.spot_it: Arabic-script Ottoman Turkish books with printed maps, from the first Ottoman Muslim-run press.
spotlights.story_md: Printing reached the Ottoman Empire early for Jewish, Armenian and Greek communities, but Ottoman Turkish books in Arabic script were not printed by Muslims until 1729. İbrahim Müteferrika, a Hungarian-born convert, got permission to print secular books such as dictionaries, histories and geographies, while religious texts stayed with scribes. His press printed 17 titles, in small editions. Historians debate why it took so long: the power of the scribes' guild, the beauty of calligraphy, the cost of making Arabic type that looked acceptable. Arabic type remained a compromise until digital shaping made joined letters look natural.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a script's beauty and social role can slow the arrival of type.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seventeen books in 1729, where Europe had printed millions.

spotlights.name: Peter the Great's civil script
spotlights.spot_it: Cyrillic letters redrawn to look like Western roman type, used for secular books.
spotlights.story_md: Before 1708, Russian books were printed in Church Slavonic letters that looked medieval. Peter the Great, modernising Russia on Western lines, personally reviewed new letter designs and crossed out characters he thought unnecessary. The resulting civil script, grazhdansky shrift, borrowed the proportions of Dutch roman type, so that secular books on science and engineering would look modern. Church books kept the old letters. Modern Cyrillic fonts descend from Peter's version. It is one of history's clearest cases of a ruler using typography as policy: change the letters, change how the nation sees itself.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Type styles can carry political meaning.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tsar edited the alphabet with his own pen.

sections.title: India's typography story
sections.intro_md:
India is home to about two dozen major scripts in daily use, which makes it one of the hardest and most interesting typographic places on Earth. Printing arrived in Goa with Jesuits in 1556, but Indian scripts were slow to get good type. Devanagari, Bengali and Tamil each have hundreds of letter combinations, and early metal fonts needed many hundreds of separate pieces.

The story runs from a blacksmith in Bengal cutting the first Bengali type, through a mission press in Serampore that printed in dozens of languages, to the hand-painted signs that still cover Indian streets, a national currency symbol chosen in an open competition, and a new generation of Indian type foundries designing for every script. In 2025 a script invented in Jharkhand joined the world's encoding standard. Here typography is not a niche craft but a question of who gets to read and write on a phone in their own language.

spotlights.name: Wilkins, Panchanan and the first Bengali type
spotlights.spot_it: A grammar of Bengali printed in 1778, the first book with Bengali letters set in movable type.
spotlights.story_md: Nathaniel Brassey Halhed, an East India Company official, wrote A Grammar of the Bengal Language and needed Bengali type to print it. Charles Wilkins, another Company servant with a gift for languages, took on the job. Working with him was Panchanan Karmakar, a blacksmith from Tribeni whose family had been engravers and calligraphers. How the work was divided is debated: older British accounts credit Wilkins, while Bengali historians argue Panchanan did much of the cutting. Panchanan later moved to Serampore and cut type for many languages. The grammar, printed in Hooghly in 1778, is a landmark of Indian printing.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It began the era of printed Indian-script books.
spotlights.memory_hook: Bengal's first type was cut by a blacksmith and a company clerk.

spotlights.name: The Serampore Mission Press
spotlights.spot_it: A Danish-controlled river town near Kolkata where missionaries printed in dozens of Asian languages.
spotlights.story_md: William Carey, Joshua Marshman and William Ward set up a press at Serampore, then a Danish settlement, because the East India Company did not allow missionaries in its territory. With Panchanan Karmakar and his son-in-law Manohar, they built type foundries for Indian scripts and printed Bible translations, grammars and dictionaries in around 40 languages. The press printed the first Bengali newspaper, Samachar Darpan, in 1818. Their fonts were used by other printers across India, and the Serampore foundry type shaped how Bengali and Devanagari looked in print for decades. The motives were religious; the effect on Indian printing was enormous.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It made Indian-language print a mass medium.
spotlights.memory_hook: A small Danish town printed in 40 Indian languages.

spotlights.name: The rupee sign
spotlights.spot_it: A Devanagari ra fused with a Latin R that has lost its stem, with two horizontal lines at the top.
spotlights.story_md: India's government held an open competition for a currency symbol and received about 3,000 entries. On 15 July 2010 the cabinet chose the design of D. Udaya Kumar, a young designer who had just joined IIT Guwahati as a teacher. The sign blends the Devanagari letter ra and the Latin capital R, and its top lines and the white space between them echo the national flag. It was added to Unicode the same year, and Indian keyboards, phones and fonts adopted it within a few years. It is a rare case of a new symbol being designed and spread to a billion people within one decade.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows a nation using a single glyph as typographic identity.
spotlights.memory_hook: One glyph, two scripts, a flag hidden in the lines.

spotlights.name: Indian Type Foundry
spotlights.spot_it: Fonts like Kohinoor that set Devanagari, Tamil or Bengali alongside matching Latin letters.
spotlights.story_md: In 2009 Satya Rajpurohit, a graduate of the National Institute of Design, and the Slovak-Dutch designer Peter Biľak started the Indian Type Foundry after finishing a Devanagari font and finding no Indian company that could distribute it in Unicode form. ITF built multi-script families such as Kohinoor, licensed by Apple among others, and released many fonts free through Google Fonts. Its success helped create a profession: Indian type design, with designers now trained at NID, IDC IIT Bombay and abroad. Other studios, such as Ek Type in Mumbai, make open-source fonts like Mukta for Indian scripts.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Indian scripts finally got professionally designed digital type at scale.
spotlights.memory_hook: The fonts in your phone's Hindi may come from Ahmedabad.

spotlights.name: Hand-painted signs and posters
spotlights.spot_it: Bold, shaded letters in two or three scripts, painted by hand on shop shutters, trucks and walls.
spotlights.story_md: Long before computers, Indian streets were lettered by sign painters who could work in Devanagari, Latin, Urdu and a regional script on the same board. They developed their own styles: drop shadows, outlined letters, decorative swashes, and the famous Horn OK Please on the backs of trucks. Bollywood posters were painted by hand in Mumbai studios until the 1990s, when vinyl flex printing took over. Many sign painters lost their livelihoods. Designers now collect, document and digitise their lettering as a vernacular tradition, and some fonts are drawn directly from it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's everyday typography, built by craftspeople without formal training.
spotlights.memory_hook: Horn OK Please is Indian typography in its natural habitat.

sections.title: Myths and half-truths
sections.intro_md:
Typography has a lot of lore, passed between designers, teachers and office managers. Some of it is good advice with a made-up history. Some is plain wrong. A few stories are stranger than the myths they replaced.

The pattern is familiar: a practical rule gets a neat origin story, the story spreads because it is memorable, and nobody checks the source. Here are three common ones, with what the evidence says.

data.claim: Two spaces after a full stop came from typewriters
data.verdict: Half true: wide sentence spaces were common in print before typewriters

data.claim: Arial is a copy of Helvetica
data.verdict: Partly: it matches Helvetica's widths but its letter shapes come from a different design
False: it is scrambled Cicero, from 45 BCE

data.claim: Times New Roman was designed to save space
data.verdict: True: narrow, compact letters for newspaper columns

data.claim: Comic Sans helps everyone with dyslexia
data.verdict: Unproven: some readers prefer it, studies do not show a general benefit

spotlights.name: One space or two
spotlights.spot_it: Two spaces after each full stop, a habit from typing classes.
spotlights.story_md: The popular story says monospaced typewriters needed two spaces after a sentence because letters were all the same width. The fuller history is messier. Many printers in the 18th and 19th centuries already used wider spaces between sentences in hand-set text, and typewriter manuals copied that practice. The switch to a single space spread in 20th-century print, and most style guides today, including the Chicago Manual of Style, ask for one. A small 2018 eye-tracking study found a slight benefit to two spaces for readers who already used two. It is less a rule of legibility than a matter of convention.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a clean example of how typographic habits are cultural.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two spaces is a habit from before the typewriter, not just because of it.

spotlights.name: Arial
spotlights.spot_it: Looks like Helvetica at a glance, but the R has a curved leg and the t and r have slanted cuts.
spotlights.story_md: Robin Nicholas and Patricia Saunders designed Arial for Monotype in 1982. It was made so that each letter takes exactly the same width as in Helvetica, so documents could be printed on cheaper laser printers without reflowing, while the shapes come from Monotype's own older grotesque designs. Microsoft licensed it for Windows in 1992 instead of paying for Helvetica, which made it one of the most used typefaces on Earth. Many designers see it as a knockoff. A fairer description is a metric-compatible substitute: designed to fit Helvetica's space, not its spirit.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how licensing and technology, not taste, often decide what fonts we see.
spotlights.memory_hook: Arial wears Helvetica's measurements but not its face.

spotlights.name: Lorem ipsum
spotlights.when: From Cicero, 45 BCE; common as placeholder since the 1960s
spotlights.spot_it: Dummy text beginning Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, used to fill layouts before the real words arrive.
spotlights.story_md: Designers use lorem ipsum so readers judge the layout, not the meaning. For years it was thought to be gibberish. In the 1990s Richard McClintock, a Latin scholar at Hampden-Sydney College, traced the rare word consectetur to Cicero's De finibus bonorum et malorum, written in 45 BCE. The text is a chopped and scrambled passage about pain: the original dolorem ipsum, pain itself, lost its first letters. The common version spread through Letraset transfer sheets in the 1960s and then desktop publishing software. So the world's most common placeholder is a philosophy lecture about why no one loves pain for its own sake.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It reminds designers that fake content hides real problems with real words.
spotlights.memory_hook: The world's dummy text is Cicero on pain, with the pain cut off.

sections.title: What is happening now
sections.intro_md:
Typography is having a busy few years. Fonts have become political markers, with a government changing its official typeface twice in under three years. The world's encoding standard keeps adding scripts used by small communities, including one from Jharkhand, which matters because a script without Unicode support cannot be typed on a phone. Big companies keep commissioning custom typefaces to save licence fees and strengthen their brands, and the type industry is consolidating, with Monotype buying foundries in Asia.

Alongside, the old questions return in new form: which fonts help people with low vision or dyslexia, whether AI tools that generate letterforms will change the craft, and how to make a page readable on screens from a watch to a television. These items are dated so you can see how fresh they are.

spotlights.name: The State Department's font reversal
spotlights.spot_it: Official US diplomatic memos in 14-point Times New Roman, then Calibri, then Times New Roman again.
spotlights.story_md: In January 2023 Secretary of State Antony Blinken ordered the department to switch from Times New Roman to Calibri, saying a sans serif without decorative features was easier to read for people with low vision or dyslexia and with screen readers. In December 2025 his successor, Marco Rubio, ordered a return to Times New Roman, describing the earlier move as a diversity programme that had degraded official correspondence. Documents for treaties and presidential appointments, which use Courier New, were exempt. Accessibility researchers note the evidence that either face is clearly better for those readers is thin. The case shows typefaces now carry political meaning.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Font choice has become a symbol in culture wars.
spotlights.memory_hook: Times New Roman, then Calibri, then Times New Roman: diplomacy by font.

spotlights.name: Tolong Siki enters Unicode
spotlights.spot_it: A script for the Kurukh language with its own letter shapes, now with a Unicode block from U+11DB0.
spotlights.story_md: Kurukh is a Dravidian language spoken by about 2.3 million people, mostly Oraon communities in Jharkhand and neighbouring states. Dr Narayan Oraon of Gumla district designed a script for it, Tolong Siki, developed from the late 1980s and formally published in 1999; Jharkhand recognised it in 2007. Unicode 17.0, released on 9 September 2025, encoded it, along with three other new scripts, bringing the total to 172 and the character count to 159,801. Encoding is only the first step: fonts, keyboards and phone support must follow before people can easily text in it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Getting a script into Unicode is now how a writing system joins the digital world.
spotlights.memory_hook: A script from a Jharkhand doctor now sits next to Latin and Chinese in every phone's standard.

spotlights.name: The web's font shift
spotlights.spot_it: Sites loading their own fonts instead of whatever the device has, often a single variable file.
spotlights.story_md: HTTP Archive's annual Web Almanac crawls millions of websites. Its 2025 fonts chapter found web fonts on about 88% of sites, and self-hosting rather than Google's servers as the most common way of serving them. Variable fonts appeared on about a third of pages in 2024, up from 28% of desktop pages in 2022. Meanwhile, big brands from banks to streaming services commission custom typefaces, partly to cut licensing bills for fonts on millions of devices. For readers, the change is mostly invisible, which, as Beatrice Warde would point out, is the point.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The web finally has typography close to print quality.
spotlights.memory_hook: Nine in ten websites now bring their own fonts.

sections.title: Recap: what typography is for
sections.intro_md:
Typography does five jobs. First, it makes language legible: you can tell the letters apart, at the size, distance and light in which you meet them. Second, it makes text readable over time, through line length, spacing and hierarchy, so reading a page does not tire you. Third, it gives words a voice, so the tone of the letters matches the message. Fourth, it organises information: headings, tables, signs and ballots tell you where to look and what to do, and bad layout can steer you wrong. Fifth, it carries identity, from the London Underground to the rupee sign, and sometimes politics.

The best typography usually goes unnoticed, as Warde said. But you now know where to look: the x-height, the serifs, the length of a line, the space between them, and the story behind the face. Next time a font annoys you, you will probably be able to say why.

cards.front: Who threw the Doves Type into the Thames, and when?
cards.back: Thomas Cobden-Sanderson, from Hammersmith Bridge, 1916 to 1917, so his ex-partner could not have it.

cards.front: Which typeface was printed on this page before its maker drowned it?
cards.back: The Doves Type, in the Doves Press Bible.

cards.front: What is Beatrice Warde's 'crystal goblet' argument?
cards.back: Printing should be like a clear wine glass: it should reveal the words, not draw attention to itself.

cards.front: Warde wrote about type history under the male pen name Paul ____.
cards.back: Beaujon.

cards.front: Legibility versus readability?
cards.back: Legibility: telling letters apart. Readability: how comfortable a whole text is to read, driven by spacing, line length and size.

cards.front: Typeface versus font?
cards.back: Typeface is the design (Garamond). Font is one specific set of it (Garamond Italic 12 point). Song versus recording.

cards.front: A comfortable line of text holds about __ to __ characters, with 66 as the classic ideal.
Why is line spacing called leading?
cards.back: Hand compositors put thin strips of lead between lines of metal type to open them up.

cards.front: What is the x-height, and why does it matter?
cards.back: The height of a lowercase x. A large x-height makes a face look bigger and read better at small sizes.

cards.front: Edward Catich's theory of where serifs came from?
cards.back: Roman sign writers painted letters with a flat brush before carving, leaving flared stroke ends that carvers cut into stone.

cards.front: What is kerning? What is a ligature?
cards.back: Kerning adjusts space between specific letter pairs (AV, To). A ligature fuses letters into one glyph (fi, fl, and & from et).

cards.front: Which monument's lettering is this, the model for countless capital letters?
cards.back: The inscription on the base of Trajan's Column, Rome, 113 CE.

cards.front: Who made the first known movable type, from what?
cards.back: Bi Sheng, in China, around the 1040s, from baked clay. Recorded by Shen Kuo.

cards.front: What is Jikji and where is it now?
cards.back: The oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, Korea, 1377. Held in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, Paris.

cards.front: Name this book.
cards.back: The Gutenberg Bible, Mainz, about 1455: 42 lines per column.

cards.front: How many Gutenberg Bibles were printed, and how many survived?
cards.back: About 180 (about 145 paper, 35 vellum). 49 survived into the 20th century, 21 complete.

cards.front: Why is Nicolas Jenson important?
cards.back: His 1470 Venetian roman type set the model for the everyday lowercase of book typefaces.

cards.front: Why was italic type first created?
cards.back: Aldus Manutius and Francesco Griffo used narrow italic in 1501 to fit classics like Virgil into small, cheap books.

cards.front: What did Benjamin Franklin's Baskerville prank prove?
cards.back: A critic said Baskerville's type hurt his eyes; Franklin showed him another founder's type labelled as Baskerville, and he found it painful too.

cards.front: Whose type specimen is this?
cards.back: Giambattista Bodoni's: extreme thick and thin contrast.

cards.front: Old-style, transitional, modern: what changes?
cards.back: The stress becomes upright and contrast grows: Garamond, then Baskerville, then Bodoni.

cards.front: Where do 'upper case' and 'lower case' come from?
cards.back: Printers' type cases: capitals in the upper case, small letters in the lower case.

cards.front: Name this machine that cast whole lines of type in hot lead.
cards.back: The Linotype, first used at the New-York Tribune in 1886.

cards.front: Linotype operators fixing errors produced the nonsense phrase etaoin ______.
cards.back: shrdlu.

cards.front: What did Steve Jobs credit with the Mac's typography?
cards.back: A calligraphy class he sat in on after dropping out of Reed College.

cards.front: Which typeface is on the Apollo 11 Moon plaque?
cards.back: Futura, designed by Paul Renner, 1927.

cards.front: Where does the name Helvetica come from?
cards.back: Latin for Switzerland. Released as Neue Haas Grotesk in 1957, renamed in 1960 to sell abroad.

cards.front: Who commissioned Times New Roman and when did it debut?
cards.back: The Times of London, with Stanley Morison; first used 3 October 1932.

cards.front: Jan Tschichold's U-turn?
cards.back: He wrote Die neue Typographie (1928) demanding sans serif and asymmetry, then after fleeing the Nazis returned to classical layouts and redesigned Penguin Books.

cards.front: Which of these is Helvetica, and which is Times New Roman?
cards.back: Helvetica is the sans serif; Times New Roman has serifs and thick-thin contrast.

cards.front: Whose 1916 lettering appears on this sign?
cards.back: Edward Johnston's, for the London Underground.

cards.front: Who designed Britain's road sign typeface Transport?
cards.back: Jock Kinneir and Margaret Calvert, 1957 to 1965.

cards.front: What happened to Clearview?
cards.back: Approved for US highways 2004, withdrawn 2016, reinstated by Congress in 2018.

cards.front: Do we read words by their outline shape?
cards.back: Mostly no. Research reviewed by Kevin Larson (2004) shows we recognise the letters in a word in parallel.

cards.front: Do dyslexia fonts improve reading?
cards.back: Studies (Kuster 2017, 170 children) found no benefit from the letterforms; spacing effects are mixed.

cards.front: Did Sans Forgetica improve memory?
cards.back: No benefit in three preregistered experiments (Geller et al., 2020).

cards.front: In Errol Morris's 2012 font test, which face won agreement and which lost?
cards.back: Baskerville did best; Comic Sans worst. About 45,000 readers.

cards.front: Why was Comic Sans created?
cards.back: A cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob spoke in Times New Roman; Vincent Connare thought it needed a casual face (1994).

cards.front: Which 2012 scientific announcement was famously set in Comic Sans?
cards.back: CERN's Higgs boson results, presented by Fabiola Gianotti on 4 July 2012.

cards.front: What was Verdanagate?
cards.back: IKEA's 2009 switch from a Futura-based face to Verdana, which angered designers.

cards.front: Who designed Verdana and Georgia, and what was unusual about the process?
cards.back: Matthew Carter, 1996, for Microsoft. He drew the pixel versions first.

cards.front: Google's Noto fonts are named after 'no more ____', the empty boxes shown for missing characters.
cards.back: tofu.

cards.front: Zuzana Licko's famous line?
cards.back: We read best what we read most.

cards.front: How did the butterfly ballot matter in 2000?
cards.back: Its layout led an estimated 2,000+ Gore voters in Palm Beach to punch Buchanan; Bush won Florida by 537.

cards.front: Why was Calibri evidence in Pakistan's Panama Papers case?
cards.back: A trust deed dated 2006 was set in Calibri, not commercially released until 2007.

cards.front: What gave away the Killian memos in 2004?
cards.back: Proportional spacing and a superscript th that matched Microsoft Word defaults, not 1970s typewriters.

cards.front: Why are Hangul's consonants shaped as they are?
cards.back: They depict the mouth and tongue position for each sound (King Sejong, 1443).

cards.front: What was the MingKwai?
cards.back: Lin Yutang's 1947 Chinese typewriter that selected characters from candidates; prototype rediscovered 2025.

cards.front: First book printed with Bengali movable type?
cards.back: Halhed's Grammar of the Bengal Language, Hooghly, 1778, type by Charles Wilkins and Panchanan Karmakar.

cards.front: Who designed this symbol, and when was it adopted?
cards.back: D. Udaya Kumar; adopted 15 July 2010.

cards.front: What is Tolong Siki?
cards.back: A script for the Kurukh language created by Dr Narayan Oraon in Jharkhand; added to Unicode 17.0 in September 2025.

cards.front: Where does lorem ipsum come from?
cards.back: A scrambled passage of Cicero's De finibus, 45 BCE, about pain.

cards.front: Is Arial a copy of Helvetica?
cards.back: It copies Helvetica's letter widths so documents fit the same space, but its shapes differ (curved R leg, slanted t and r cuts).

cards.front: What did the US State Department do with fonts in 2023 and 2025?
cards.back: Switched from Times New Roman to Calibri in 2023, back to Times New Roman in December 2025.

cards.front: This red, white and blue sign shows which city's transport identity?
cards.back: London's: the Underground roundel with Johnston lettering.

cards.front: Name the font on this page of a long-gone computer interface.
cards.back: Chicago, Susan Kare's bitmap font for the 1984 Macintosh.

cards.front: Which writing system is this book announcing?
cards.back: Hangul, in the Hunminjeongeum, 1446.

cards.front: What kind of sign is this, and who designed its letters?
cards.back: A British road sign in Transport, by Kinneir and Calvert.

cards.front: Which typeface is this?
cards.back: Comic Sans.

cards.front: What is this, and when was it printed?
cards.back: Jikji, the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type, 1377.

cards.front: What is this object, and what text is set on it?
